% ================================================================
% Quick Questions deck: factors, multiples and primes.
%
% Each topic opens with five true/false statements and then runs ten
% quick questions that get gradually harder. Every question gets two
% slides: the question on its own for the mini whiteboards, then the
% same question again with the solution underneath in red.
%
% Two topics are built differently. "Is it prime?" runs every whole
% number from 1 to 100 on its own slide, then lists that number's
% factors and says why it is or is not prime. "HCF and LCM from lists"
% builds each answer over five slides, adding the factor lists, the
% multiples and then the rings round the HCF and the LCM one slide at
% a time.
% ================================================================

\setbeamertemplate{navigation symbols}{}

% A link in the bottom left of every slide back to the contents, so a
% deck this long can be jumped around in during a lesson.
\setbeamertemplate{footline}{%
  \hbox to\paperwidth{%
    \hspace{1em}%
    \hyperlink{contents}{%
      \color{gray}\scriptsize$\leftarrow$~Back to contents}%
    \hfil}%
  \vskip4pt%
}

% Topic divider.
\newcommand{\qtopic}[1]{%
  \section{#1}%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      {\usebeamercolor[fg]{structure}\Huge\bfseries #1}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
}

% \qq[<question size>][<solution size>]{<question>}{<solution>}
% The two optional sizes drop the type for the wordier questions and
% the longer solutions, so nothing runs off the slide.
\NewDocumentCommand{\qq}{O{\Huge}O{\LARGE}+m+m}{%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      \begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
        \centering #1 #3
      \end{minipage}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      \begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
        \centering #1 #3
        \par\vspace{0.9em}
        {\color{red}#2 #4}
      \end{minipage}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
}

% \tf[<statement size>][<answer size>]{<statement>}{<answer>}
% As \qq, but with a standing "True or false?" heading above the
% statement. The statements hunt for the usual misconceptions, so the
% answer always says why, not just which.
\NewDocumentCommand{\tf}{O{\LARGE}O{\Large}+m+m}{%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      \begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
        \centering
        {\usebeamercolor[fg]{structure}\Large\bfseries True or false?}
        \par\vspace{1em}
        #1 #3
      \end{minipage}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      \begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
        \centering
        {\usebeamercolor[fg]{structure}\Large\bfseries True or false?}
        \par\vspace{1em}
        #1 #3
        \par\vspace{0.9em}
        {\color{red}#2 #4}
      \end{minipage}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
}

% \prq{<number>}{<factors>}{<why it is or is not prime>}
% The "Is it prime?" drill: the number alone in a large centred font,
% then the same number with all of its factors and the reason in red.
% The number is scaled rather than set with \fontsize, because the
% sans font stops at 51.59pt and larger sizes are silently substituted.
\NewDocumentCommand{\prq}{m m +m}{%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      \scalebox{3.6}{\Huge\bfseries #1}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
  \begin{frame}
    \vfill
    \begin{center}
      \scalebox{1.9}{\Huge\bfseries #1}
      \par\vspace{0.8em}
      \begin{minipage}{0.9\textwidth}
        \centering\color{red}
        {\large Factors of $#1$: #2}
        \par\vspace{0.7em}
        {\large #3}
      \end{minipage}
    \end{center}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
}

% Rings drawn round a number in a list. The ring is set in a box the
% width of the number itself, so the list is spaced as though it were
% ordinary text and nothing moves on the slide where the ring appears;
% the ring itself spills over the gaps either side, as a ring drawn by
% hand would.
\tikzset{
  ringed/.style={ellipse, inner sep=1pt, draw=red, line width=0.9pt},
  unringed/.style={ellipse, inner sep=1pt, draw=none},
}
\newlength{\ringwd}
\newcommand{\ringnode}[2]{%
  \settowidth{\ringwd}{$#2$}%
  \addtolength{\ringwd}{3pt}% a little clearance for the ring to sit in
  \makebox[\ringwd][c]{%
    \tikz[baseline=(n.base)]{\node[#1] (n) {$#2$};}%
  }%
}
\newcommand{\hcfmark}[1]{\alt<4->{\ringnode{ringed}{#1}}{\ringnode{unringed}{#1}}}
\newcommand{\lcmmark}[1]{\alt<5->{\ringnode{ringed}{#1}}{\ringnode{unringed}{#1}}}

% \hcflcm{<a>}{<b>}{<factors of a>}{<factors of b>}
%        {<multiples of a>}{<multiples of b>}
% Five slides: the question, the two factor lists, the two lists of
% multiples, the ring round the HCF, then the ring round the LCM.
% Everything added after the question slide is in red.
% The frame is top aligned so that the question stays put as the lists
% are added underneath it.
\NewDocumentCommand{\hcflcm}{m m +m +m +m +m}{%
  \begin{frame}<1-5>[t]
    \vspace{0.8em}
    \begin{center}
      {\LARGE Find the HCF and LCM of $#1$ and $#2$.}
    \end{center}
    \vspace{1.6em}
    \begin{columns}[T]
      \begin{column}{0.40\textwidth}
        \only<2->{\color{red}\large
          Factors of $#1$:\\[0.35em]
          #3
          \par\vspace{1em}
          Factors of $#2$:\\[0.35em]
          #4}
      \end{column}
      \begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
        \only<3->{\color{red}\large
          Multiples of $#1$:\\[0.35em]
          #5
          \par\vspace{1em}
          Multiples of $#2$:\\[0.35em]
          #6}
      \end{column}
    \end{columns}
    \vfill
  \end{frame}%
}

% Contents-slide bullets. Green then orange sets the difficulty band;
% blue marks the two topics that work through a method a slide at a
% time rather than asking for a quick answer.
\newcommand{\tocbullet}[1]{\textcolor{#1}{$\bullet$}}
\setbeamertemplate{section in toc}{%
  \ifcase\inserttocsectionnumber
    \or\tocbullet{green!55!black}% 1 Factors
    \or\tocbullet{green!55!black}% 2 Multiples
    \or\tocbullet{green!55!black}% 3 Primes
    \or\tocbullet{blue}%          4 Is it prime?
    \or\tocbullet{orange}%        5 Prime factor decomposition
    \or\tocbullet{blue}%          6 HCF and LCM from lists
    \or\tocbullet{orange}%        7 HCF and LCM by prime factor decomposition
    \or\tocbullet{orange}%        8 Square numbers from prime factors
    \or\tocbullet{orange}%        9 Problem solving with HCF and LCM
  \fi
  ~\inserttocsection%
}

% a tier 3 word, in English and in translation alike
\newcommand{\ealkey}[1]{\textcolor{ealkeycolour}{#1}}
\newcommand{\ealkeytr}[1]{\textcolor{ealkeycolour}{\ealtext{#1}}}

% One translated word above one English word. Built from kernel
% primitives, never a tabular, which would break wherever the sheet
% loads array, booktabs or tabularx. The box is as wide as the wider of
% the two, so a long translation pushes its neighbours aside instead of
% overlapping them, and it claims its full height so a table row or a
% TikZ node makes room for it.
\newcommand{\ealgloss}[2]{%
  \sbox{\ealboxen}{\ealkey{#1}}%
  \sbox{\ealboxtr}{\small\textcolor{ealtwocolour}{\ealtext{#2}}}%
  \setlength{\ealglosswd}{\wd\ealboxen}%
  \ifdim\wd\ealboxtr>\ealglosswd\setlength{\ealglosswd}{\wd\ealboxtr}\fi
  \leavevmode
  \makebox[\ealglosswd][c]{%
    \makebox[0pt][c]{\usebox{\ealboxen}}%
    \makebox[0pt][c]{\raisebox{\ealglossraise}{\usebox{\ealboxtr}}}%
  }%
}

% opens up line spacing around a block of glosses, so the raised
% translations sit clear of the line above
\newenvironment{ealglossed}{\par\linespread{2.1}\selectfont\ignorespaces}{\par}

% a whole translated sentence above its English counterpart. block level,
% so it does not belong inside a tabular cell
\newcommand{\ealpara}[2]{%
  \par\addvspace{0.5\baselineskip}%
  {\color{ealtwocolour}\ealtextblock{#1}}%
  \penalty200
  {\color{ealenglish}#2\par}%
  \addvspace{0.5\baselineskip}%
}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Factors}{\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$7$ is a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of $21$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{True.} $21=7\times 3$, so $21$ divides exactly by $7$.}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$1$ is a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of every whole number\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{True.} Every number $n$ can be written as $1\times n$.}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$6$ is a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of $16$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} The \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} of $16$ are $1,2,4,8,16$;\\[0.3em]
   $16\div 6$ is not a whole number.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}Every number has an even number of \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} \ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل} usually pair up, but $9$ has just $1,3,9$
   --- three \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} --- because $3\times 3$ uses the same \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} twice.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}If $4$ is a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of a number,\\[0.3em]then $8$ must be a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of it too\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} $4$ is a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of $12$, but $8$ is not.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}List all the \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} of $12$\end{ealglossed}}{$1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6,\ 12$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}List all the \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} of $20$\end{ealglossed}}{$1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 5,\ 10,\ 20$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}List all the \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} of $36$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6,\ 9,\ 12,\ 18,\ 36$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}How many \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} does $16$ have?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 8,\ 16$\\[0.3em]Five \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{highest common factor}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of $12$ and $18$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل} of $12$: $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ \mathbf{6},\ 12$\\[0.3em]
   \ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل} of $18$: $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ \mathbf{6},\ 9,\ 18$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=6$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{highest common factor}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of $24$ and $36$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل} of $24$: $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6,\ 8,\ \mathbf{12},\ 24$\\[0.3em]
   \ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل} of $36$: $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6,\ 9,\ \mathbf{12},\ 18,\ 36$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=12$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}List all the \ealgloss{factor pairs}{عوامل کے جوڑے} of $48$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$1\times 48\qquad 2\times 24\qquad 3\times 16$\\[0.4em]
   $4\times 12\qquad 6\times 8$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Which whole number below $30$ has the most \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$24$, with eight \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}:\\[0.3em]
   $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6,\ 8,\ 12,\ 24$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}$n$ has exactly three \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}.\\[0.4em]
Give a possible value of $n$.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$4$ ($1,2,4$), $9$ ($1,3,9$) or $25$ ($1,5,25$).\\[0.3em]
   Any \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} squared works.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Explain why \ealgloss{square numbers}{مربع اعداد} have an odd number of \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Factors}{عوامل} come in pairs, one either side of the \ealgloss{square root}{جذر}.\\[0.3em]
   In a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد} the \ealgloss{square root}{جذر} pairs with itself,
   so one \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} is left unpaired.\end{ealglossed}}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Multiples}{\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Multiples}{مضاعفات}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$24$ is a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $6$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{True.} $6\times 4=24$.}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}Every \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $10$ is also a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $5$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} $10=5\times 2$, so every \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $10$
   already contains a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of $5$.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$35$ is a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $4$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{False.} $4\times 8=32$ and $4\times 9=36$, so $35$ is stepped over.}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}Every \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $3$ is also a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $9$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} $6$ is a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $3$ but not of $9$.\\[0.3em]
   The other way round \emph{is} true.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{lowest common multiple}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of two numbers is always found by
multiplying them together\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} $4\times 6=24$, but the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $4$ and $6$ is $12$.\\[0.3em]
   Multiplying only works when the numbers share no \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write down the first five \ealgloss{multiples}{مضاعفات} of $4$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$4,\ 8,\ 12,\ 16,\ 20$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write down the first five \ealgloss{multiples}{مضاعفات} of $7$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$7,\ 14,\ 21,\ 28,\ 35$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write down the \ealgloss{multiples}{مضاعفات} of $6$ between $20$ and $50$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$24,\ 30,\ 36,\ 42,\ 48$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Is $126$ a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $9$?\end{ealglossed}}
  {Yes. $1+2+6=9$, and $9\times 14=126$.}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{lowest common multiple}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $4$ and $6$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$4,\ 8,\ \mathbf{12},\ 16,\ \ldots$\\[0.3em]
   $6,\ \mathbf{12},\ 18,\ \ldots$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=12$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{lowest common multiple}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $8$ and $12$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$8,\ 16,\ \mathbf{24},\ 32,\ \ldots$\\[0.3em]
   $12,\ \mathbf{24},\ 36,\ \ldots$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=24$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{lowest common multiple}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $5$, $6$ and $9$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $5$ and $6$ is $30$.\\[0.3em]
   \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $30$ and $9$ is $90$.\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=90$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}A number is a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of both $4$ and $10$.\\[0.4em]
What is the smallest it could be?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$20$, the \ealgloss{lowest common multiple}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $4$ and $10$.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Two lighthouses flash together now.\\[0.4em]
One flashes every $12$ seconds, the other every $18$ seconds.\\[0.4em]
When do they next flash together?}
  {$\mathrm{LCM}(12,18)=36$\\[0.3em]
   In $36$ seconds.}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Find the smallest number above $1$ that leaves a remainder
of $1$ when divided by $4$, by $5$ and by $6$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}The number must be one more than a common \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of $4$, $5$ and $6$.\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}(4,5,6)=60$, so the number is $61$.\end{ealglossed}}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Primes}{\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Primes}{مفرد اعداد}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$1$ is a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} A \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} has exactly two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, but $1$ has only one.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$2$ is the only even \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} Every other even number has $2$ as an extra \ealgloss{factor}{عامل},
   so it has more than two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}$51$ is a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{False.} $51=3\times 17$.\\[0.3em]
   Its digits add to $6$, so it divides by $3$.}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}There are infinitely many \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} numbers\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} The \ealgloss{primes}{مفرد اعداد} never run out,
   although they do thin out as the numbers get larger.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf{\begin{ealglossed}If a number ends in $3$, it must be \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{False.} $33=3\times 11$ and $63=7\times 9$.}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write down all the \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} numbers between $1$ and $10$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write down all the \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} numbers between $10$ and $20$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$11,\ 13,\ 17,\ 19$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Is $27$ a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number?\\[0.4em]Explain your answer.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}No. $27=3\times 9$, so it has more than two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write down the first \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number greater than $30$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$31$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Is $91$ a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number?\end{ealglossed}}
  {No. $91=7\times 13$.}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}How many \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} numbers are there between $20$ and $40$?\end{ealglossed}}
  {$23,\ 29,\ 31,\ 37$\\[0.3em]Four of them.}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Is $143$ a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number?\end{ealglossed}}
  {No. $143=11\times 13$.}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Find two \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} numbers that add up to $24$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$5+19$ \quad $7+17$ \quad $11+13$}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}To test whether $211$ is \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد},\\[0.3em]
which numbers do you need to divide by?\\[0.4em]Is it \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Only the \ealgloss{primes}{مفرد اعداد} up to $\sqrt{211}\approx 14.5$:\\[0.3em]
   $2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 11,\ 13$\\[0.3em]
   None of them divides $211$, so $211$ is \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Explain why $n^2-1$ can never be \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} when $n>2$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$n^2-1=(n-1)(n+1)$\\[0.3em]
   When $n>2$ both brackets are bigger than $1$,
   so the number always has more than two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}.\end{ealglossed}}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Is it prime?}{\begin{ealglossed}Is it \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}?\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\prq{1}{$1$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$1$ has only one \ealgloss{factor}{عامل}. A \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number has exactly two different \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, $1$ and itself, and for $1$ those would be the same \ealgloss{factor}{عامل}, so $1$ is not a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number.\end{ealglossed}}

\prq{2}{$1$, $2$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$2$ has exactly two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, $1$ and itself, so $2$ is a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number. It is the only even \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number, because every other even number has $2$ as a third \ealgloss{factor}{عامل}.\end{ealglossed}}

\prq{3}{$1$, $3$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$3$ has exactly two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, $1$ and itself, so $3$ is a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number.\end{ealglossed}}

\prq{4}{$1$, $2$, $4$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$4$ has three \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, not two, so $4$ is not a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number.\end{ealglossed}}

\prq{5}{$1$, $5$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$5$ has exactly two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, $1$ and itself, so $5$ is a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number.\\[0.45em]We only need to test $2$ as a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل}, because $3\times 3=9$ is bigger than $5$.\end{ealglossed}}

\prq{6}{$1$, $2$, $3$, $6$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$6$ has four \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, not two, so $6$ is not a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number.\end{ealglossed}}

  {\begin{ealglossed}$7$ has exactly two \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}, $1$ and itself, so $7$ is a \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} number.\\[0.45em]We only need to test $2$ as a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل}, because $3\times 3=9$ is bigger than $7$.\end{ealglossed}}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Prime factor decomposition}{\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{Prime factor decomposition}{مفرد عوامل میں تحلیل}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$12=2^2\times 3$ is the \ealgloss{prime factor decomposition}{مفرد عوامل میں تحلیل} of $12$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} $2$ and $3$ are both \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد},
   and $4\times 3=12$.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$2\times 3\times 4$ is the \ealgloss{prime factor decomposition}{مفرد عوامل میں تحلیل} of $24$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} $4$ is not \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}.\\[0.3em]
   $24=2^3\times 3$\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Every whole number greater than $1$ can be written as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب}
of \ealgloss{primes}{مفرد اعداد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} A \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} is its own decomposition, and any other number
   keeps splitting until only \ealgloss{primes}{مفرد اعداد} are left.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}A number can have two different \ealgloss{prime factor decompositions}{مفرد عوامل میں تحلیل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{False.} Apart from the order you write them in,
   every number has exactly one decomposition.}

\tf[\Large]{$2^3\times 5=30$}
  {\textbf{False.} $2^3\times 5=8\times 5=40$.\\[0.3em]
   $30=2\times 3\times 5$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $12$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$12=2\times 2\times 3=2^2\times 3$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $18$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$18=2\times 3\times 3=2\times 3^2$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $60$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$60=2\times 2\times 3\times 5=2^2\times 3\times 5$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $84$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$84=2\times 2\times 3\times 7=2^2\times 3\times 7$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $200$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$200=2\times 2\times 2\times 5\times 5=2^3\times 5^2$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $360$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$360=2^3\times 3^2\times 5$}

\qq[\LARGE]{\begin{ealglossed}Write $1001$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of its \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {$1001=7\times 143=7\times 11\times 13$}

\qq[\LARGE]{Work out $2^3\times 3\times 5^2$ as an ordinary number}
  {$8\times 3\times 25=600$}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$n=2^3\times 3\times 5$.\\[0.4em]
Write $2n$ as a \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Doubling adds one more \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of $2$:\\[0.3em]
   $2n=2^4\times 3\times 5$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$720=2^4\times 3^2\times 5$.\\[0.4em]
How many \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل} does $720$ have?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Each \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} uses $0$ to $4$ twos, $0$ to $2$ threes and $0$ or $1$ five:\\[0.3em]
   $5\times 3\times 2=30$ \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}

\qtopic{HCF and LCM by prime factor decomposition}{\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} and \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} by \ealgloss{prime factor decomposition}{مفرد عوامل میں تحلیل}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of two numbers is always smaller than both of them\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} The \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of $6$ and $12$ is $6$,
   which is one of the numbers itself.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of two numbers is always a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of both of them\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} That is exactly what a common \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} is;
   the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} is the smallest one.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}If $a=2^2\times 3$ and $b=2\times 3^2$,\\[0.3em]then the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of
$a$ and $b$ is $2\times 3$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} Take the \emph{lowest} \ealgloss{power}{قوت} of each \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} that appears
   in both: $2^1\times 3^1=6$.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$\mathrm{HCF}\times\mathrm{LCM}$ gives the \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of the two numbers\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} Every \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد} is counted once at its lowest \ealgloss{power}{قوت} and once
   at its highest, which is the same as counting both numbers.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{lowest common multiple}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $6$ and $8$ is $48$\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} $6=2\times 3$ and $8=2^3$,
   so the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} is $2^3\times 3=24$.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$12=2^2\times 3$ \quad and \quad $18=2\times 3^2$\\[0.4em]
Find the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of $12$ and $18$.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Lowest \ealgloss{power}{قوت} of each shared \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}:\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=2\times 3=6$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$12=2^2\times 3$ \quad and \quad $18=2\times 3^2$\\[0.4em]
Find the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $12$ and $18$.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Highest \ealgloss{power}{قوت} of each \ealgloss{prime}{مفرد عدد}:\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=2^2\times 3^2=36$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$24=2^3\times 3$ \quad and \quad $60=2^2\times 3\times 5$\\[0.4em]
Find the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} of $24$ and $60$.\end{ealglossed}}
  {$\mathrm{HCF}=2^2\times 3=12$}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$24=2^3\times 3$ \quad and \quad $60=2^2\times 3\times 5$\\[0.4em]
Find the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $24$ and $60$.\end{ealglossed}}
  {$\mathrm{LCM}=2^3\times 3\times 5=120$}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} and the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $84$ and $120$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$84=2^2\times 3\times 7$ \qquad $120=2^3\times 3\times 5$\\[0.4em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=2^2\times 3=12$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=2^3\times 3\times 5\times 7=840$}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} and the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of $126$ and $180$\end{ealglossed}}
  {$126=2\times 3^2\times 7$ \qquad $180=2^2\times 3^2\times 5$\\[0.4em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=2\times 3^2=18$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=2^2\times 3^2\times 5\times 7=1260$}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}$a=2^3\times 3^2\times 5$ \quad and \quad
$b=2^2\times 3\times 5^2$\\[0.4em]
Find the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} and the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف}, in \ealgloss{index form}{قوت نما شکل}.\end{ealglossed}}
  {$\mathrm{HCF}=2^2\times 3\times 5$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=2^3\times 3^2\times 5^2$}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}Two numbers have \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} $6$ and \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} $72$.\\[0.4em]
One of the numbers is $24$. Find the other.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$\mathrm{HCF}\times\mathrm{LCM}=6\times 72=432$, which is the
   \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} of the two numbers.\\[0.4em]
   $432\div 24=18$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}Find the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} and the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of\\[0.4em]
$2^5\times 3^2\times 11$ \quad and \quad $2^3\times 3^4\times 7$\\[0.4em]
Leave your answers in \ealgloss{index form}{قوت نما شکل}.\end{ealglossed}}
  {$\mathrm{HCF}=2^3\times 3^2$\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=2^5\times 3^4\times 7\times 11$}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}Two numbers have \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} $12$ and \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} $180$.\\[0.4em]
Find the numbers. Is there more than one answer?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Their \ealgloss{product}{حاصل ضرب} is $12\times 180=2160$, and both are \ealgloss{multiples}{مضاعفات} of $12$.\\[0.4em]
   $12$ and $180$ \quad or \quad $36$ and $60$\\[0.3em]
   Both pairs work, so there is more than one answer.\end{ealglossed}}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Square numbers from prime factors}{\begin{ealglossed}\ealgloss{square numbers}{مربع اعداد} from \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}A number is square exactly when every \ealgloss{power}{قوت} in its \ealgloss{prime factor decomposition}{مفرد عوامل میں تحلیل} is even\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} Halving every even \ealgloss{power}{قوت} gives the \ealgloss{square root}{جذر}.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$2^3\times 3^2$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} The \ealgloss{power}{قوت} of $2$ is odd,
   so the number cannot be split into two equal halves.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}$2^4\times 5^6$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\textbf{True.} $2^4\times 5^6=\left(2^2\times 5^3\right)^2$}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Every \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد} has an even number of \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} \ealgloss{Square numbers}{مربع اعداد} have an \emph{odd} number of \ealgloss{factors}{عوامل}:\\[0.3em]
   $16$ has $1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 8,\ 16$.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}If $n$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}, then $4n$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد} too\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} Multiplying by $4=2^2$ keeps every \ealgloss{power}{قوت} even.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Use \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل} to show that $36$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$36=2^2\times 3^2$\\[0.3em]
   Both \ealgloss{powers}{قوتیں} are even, and $36=(2\times 3)^2=6^2$.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Is $2^2\times 3^2\times 5^2$ a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}?\\[0.4em]
If so, what is its \ealgloss{square root}{جذر}?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Yes --- every \ealgloss{power}{قوت} is even.\\[0.3em]
   $\sqrt{2^2\times 3^2\times 5^2}=2\times 3\times 5=30$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Is $2^3\times 3^2$ a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}?\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}No. Halving the \ealgloss{powers}{قوتیں} would need $2^{1.5}$,\\[0.3em]
   so the \ealgloss{power}{قوت} of $2$ must be even and it is not.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Work out $\sqrt{2^6\times 3^4}$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Halve each \ealgloss{power}{قوت}:\\[0.3em]
   $2^3\times 3^2=8\times 9=72$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Use \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل} to decide whether $400$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$400=2^4\times 5^2$\\[0.3em]
   Both \ealgloss{powers}{قوتیں} are even, so $400=\left(2^2\times 5\right)^2=20^2$.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Use \ealgloss{prime factors}{مفرد عوامل} to decide whether $150$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}$150=2\times 3\times 5^2$\\[0.3em]
   The \ealgloss{powers}{قوتیں} of $2$ and $3$ are odd, so $150$ is not square.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Work out $\sqrt{2^8\times 3^2\times 5^4}$}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Halve each \ealgloss{power}{قوت}:\\[0.3em]
   $2^4\times 3\times 5^2=16\times 3\times 25=1200$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}$n=2^3\times 3\times 5^2$\\[0.4em]
Find the smallest whole number $k$ so that $nk$ is a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{powers}{قوتیں} of $2$ and $3$ are odd, so each needs one more:\\[0.3em]
   $k=2\times 3=6$, giving $nk=2^4\times 3^2\times 5^2$.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}$504=2^3\times 3^2\times 7$\\[0.4em]
Find the smallest number $504$ can be multiplied by to give a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}.\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{powers}{قوتیں} of $2$ and $7$ are odd:\\[0.3em]
   multiply by $2\times 7=14$.\\[0.3em]
   $504\times 14=7056=84^2$\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\large]{\begin{ealglossed}$1080=2^3\times 3^3\times 5$\\[0.4em]
Find the smallest number $1080$ can be divided by to give a \ealgloss{square number}{مربع عدد}.\end{ealglossed}}
  {Remove one $2$, one $3$ and the $5$:\\[0.3em]
   divide by $2\times 3\times 5=30$.\\[0.3em]
   $1080\div 30=36=6^2$}

%================================================================
\qtopic{Problem solving with HCF and LCM}{\begin{ealglossed}Problem solving with \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} and \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف}\end{ealglossed}}
%================================================================

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}To find when two repeating events next happen together,
you use the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} You are looking for the first time that is a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف}
   of both gaps.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}To split two collections into the largest identical bags,
you use the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{False.} Use the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل} --- the bag size has to be a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل}
   of both amounts.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}Cutting two ropes into equal pieces, as long as possible with
none left over, uses the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل}\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} The piece length must be a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of both rope lengths.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{\begin{ealglossed}The \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف} of two numbers is never smaller than either of them\end{ealglossed}}
  {\begin{ealglossed}\textbf{True.} It is a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of each number,
   so it is at least as big as both.\end{ealglossed}}

\tf[\Large]{Two events repeat every $4$ minutes and every $6$ minutes,\\[0.3em]
so they coincide every $24$ minutes}
  {\textbf{False.} They coincide every $\mathrm{LCM}(4,6)=12$ minutes.}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Two bells ring together now.\\[0.4em]
One rings every $4$ minutes, the other every $6$ minutes.\\[0.4em]
When do they next ring together?}
  {\begin{ealglossed}Common \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف}, so use the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف}:\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}(4,6)=12$ --- in $12$ minutes.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Two ribbons, $18$\,cm and $24$\,cm long, are cut into
equal pieces, as long as possible with none left over.\\[0.4em]
How long is each piece?}
  {\begin{ealglossed}The length must be a \ealgloss{factor}{عامل} of both, so use the \ealgloss{HCF}{سب سے بڑا مشترک عامل}:\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}(18,24)=6$ --- each piece is $6$\,cm.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\large]{$36$ pens and $48$ pencils are shared into identical packs
with nothing left over.\\[0.4em]
What is the greatest number of packs?}
  {$36=2^2\times 3^2$ \qquad $48=2^4\times 3$\\[0.4em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=2^2\times 3=12$ packs,\\[0.3em]
   each with $3$ pens and $4$ pencils.}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Two lighthouses flash together at $8$pm.\\[0.4em]
One flashes every $15$ seconds, the other every $18$ seconds.\\[0.4em]
When do they next flash together?}
  {$\mathrm{LCM}(15,18)=90$ seconds\\[0.3em]
   At $8${:}$01${:}$30$pm.}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{Rectangular tiles measure $12$\,cm by $18$\,cm.\\[0.4em]
What is the smallest square they can tile exactly?}
  {\begin{ealglossed}The side must be a \ealgloss{multiple}{مضاعف} of both, so use the \ealgloss{LCM}{سب سے چھوٹا مشترک مضاعف}:\\[0.3em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}(12,18)=36$\\[0.3em]
   A $36$\,cm by $36$\,cm square.\end{ealglossed}}

\qq[\Large][\Large]{A bus leaves every $24$ minutes and a tram every
$36$ minutes.\\[0.4em]
Both leave at $9${:}$00$. When do they next leave together?}
  {$\mathrm{LCM}(24,36)=72$ minutes\\[0.3em]
   At $10${:}$12$.}

\qq[\Large][\large]{Two cogs, with $18$ and $24$ teeth, start meshed at a
marked tooth.\\[0.4em]
How many turns does each make before the marks meet again?}
  {$\mathrm{LCM}(18,24)=72$ teeth must pass.\\[0.4em]
   $72\div 18=4$ turns of the small cog,\\[0.3em]
   $72\div 24=3$ turns of the large cog.}

\qq[\Large][\large]{A floor measures $360$\,cm by $504$\,cm.\\[0.4em]
It is tiled with identical square tiles, as large as possible.\\[0.4em]
Find the tile size and the number of tiles.}
  {$360=2^3\times 3^2\times 5$ \qquad $504=2^3\times 3^2\times 7$\\[0.4em]
   $\mathrm{HCF}=2^3\times 3^2=72$, so the tiles are $72$\,cm square.\\[0.3em]
   $5\times 7=35$ tiles.}

\qq[\Large][\large]{Three runners take $60$\,s, $72$\,s and $90$\,s per lap.\\[0.4em]
They start together. When are they next all at the start line?}
  {$60=2^2\times 3\times 5$ \quad $72=2^3\times 3^2$ \quad
   $90=2\times 3^2\times 5$\\[0.4em]
   $\mathrm{LCM}=2^3\times 3^2\times 5=360$\,s\\[0.3em]
   After $6$ minutes.}

\qq[\Large][\large]{Hot dogs come in packs of $10$, buns in packs of $8$ and
sauce sachets in packs of $12$.\\[0.4em]
What is the smallest number of complete hot dogs Sam can make with nothing
left over, and how many packs of each is that?}
  {$\mathrm{LCM}(10,8,12)=2^3\times 3\times 5=120$\\[0.4em]
   $120$ hot dogs: $12$ packs of hot dogs,\\[0.3em]
   $15$ packs of buns and $10$ packs of sachets.}

\end{document}
